notes:
I've written verse-by-verse notes on Galatians 6 below. Before using them, you should know where the research falls short:

- **Missing sites.** I didn't get to any Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Methodist or modern-scholarship site (newadvent, oca, lcms, 1517, wesley.nnu.edu, bibleodyssey, netbible). Where those traditions appear, it's only through older commentators quoted on biblehub, studylight or enduringword.
- **Verses 9–18 are thinner.** The Enduring Word page cut off partway through verse 7, so later verses rely more on other commentaries.
- **Verses where traditions really differ.** I found clear disagreements on verse 16 ("Israel of God") and verse 6 (paying teachers), a Protestant/Catholic difference on verse 17, and a mild disagreement on verse 11.
- **Prosperity teaching.** No page I read describes that teaching directly. What I have on verses 7–8 is traditional teachers warning against treating giving as a money-making scheme.

**v. 1**
- Guzik says "overtaken" points to someone who has fallen into a sin they didn't plan, not a hardened sinner. He quotes Luther saying Paul means faults of human weakness, not false doctrine. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/galatians-6/
- "Restore" (*katartizō*) is the word for mending nets, and was also used for setting broken or dislocated bones. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/galatians/6-1.htm
- Who are "you who are spiritual"? Gill says Paul means the church members in general, not just ministers. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/galatians/6-1.htm Matthew Henry agrees: ministers, but other Christians too. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gal/Gal_006.cfm
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown warns that people who correct others without gentleness are likely to be tempted themselves. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/galatians/6-1.htm

**v. 2**
- Guzik sees a jab at the legalists: if you want a law to keep, this is it. He cites Stott: lift other people's burdens instead of loading the law onto them. Guzik links "the law of Christ" to Jesus' command to love one another (John 13:34–35). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/galatians-6/
- Henry: Christians are free from Moses' law but under Christ's law. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gal/Gal_006.cfm
- Robertson: "bear" is the same verb used of Jesus carrying his cross. The heavy "burden" is the moment when a person's normal load is about to crush them. https://ccel.org/ccel/robertson_at/wp_gal/wp_gal.vii.html
- MacLaren: we can only bear others' burdens with Christ's sacrifice as both our hope and our example. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mac/galatians-6.html

**v. 3**
- Robertson: the word for "deceives" means to lead one's own mind astray. Such a person fools no one but himself. https://ccel.org/ccel/robertson_at/wp_gal/wp_gal.vii.html
- Boice reads the verse as explaining why some refuse to bear others' burdens: they think they're above it. https://www.preceptaustin.org/galatians-6-commentary
- Guzik quotes Calvin: since everyone is nothing, anyone who thinks he is something deceives himself. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/galatians-6/

**v. 4**
- Preceptaustin: the verb is *dokimazō*, a command to keep testing your work to prove its worth. https://www.preceptaustin.org/galatians_67_commentary
- Guzik: we should examine ourselves honestly, so our joy rests on our own walk with God rather than on feeling better than someone who has fallen. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/galatians-6/

**v. 5**
- Verses 2 and 5 don't contradict each other. Verse 2 is about caring for others; verse 5 is about our final accountability to God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/galatians-6/
- Verse 5's "load" (*phortion*) means an ordinary backpack. Verse 2's "burdens" (*barē*) are crushing weights. https://biblehub.com/galatians/6.htm
- Henry links verse 5 to the day of judgment. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gal/Gal_006.cfm Robertson notes Paul doesn't always keep the two words separate, though he does here. https://ccel.org/ccel/robertson_at/wp_gal/wp_gal.vii.html

**v. 6 (a disputed point)**
- The usual reading is that Christians should support their teachers financially. Guzik cites Lightfoot and Fung for this. He also quotes Luther saying he didn't enjoy explaining these verses, because it made him look self-interested. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/galatians-6/
- Robertson says the verse shows how early churches had paid teachers. https://ccel.org/ccel/robertson_at/wp_gal/wp_gal.vii.html
- The other view: John MacArthur says he doesn't think the verse is about paying the preacher. He takes it as continuing the theme of restoring others through teaching them the Word. https://www.preceptaustin.org/galatians-6-commentary

**v. 7**
- Spurgeon says Luther and Calvin both read verse 7 as being about how congregations treat their ministers' financial support. https://ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons54/sermons54.xxxvii.html Barnes reads it the same way. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/galatians/6-7.html
- Spurgeon himself preaches it more broadly: evil sowing brings an evil harvest. https://ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons54/sermons54.xxxvii.html
- Robertson: "mocked" literally means to turn up one's nose at someone, and nobody does that to God without consequences. https://ccel.org/ccel/robertson_at/wp_gal/wp_gal.vii.html
- Guzik says Paul isn't teaching a kind of "spiritual karma." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/galatians-6/

**v. 8 (relevant to prosperity teaching)**
- Guzik: sowing to the Spirit, even with money, doesn't necessarily bring back money. It brings something better. We don't give as a crude "investment" or money-making scheme. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/galatians-6/
- A Biblical Illustrator sermon says that a person who sows to the Spirit should expect a harvest of eternal life, "not money and pleasure." https://biblehub.com/sermons/galatians/6-7.htm
- Constable: the verse doesn't teach that a person can earn justification. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/galatians/6-7.html
- Robertson: "corruption" here means the physical and moral decay that follows sin. https://ccel.org/ccel/robertson_at/wp_gal/wp_gal.vii.html

**v. 9**
- Robertson: "grow weary" literally means giving in to evil while doing good. "In due time" means at harvest time, and "give up" pictures someone exhausted and slack. https://ccel.org/ccel/robertson_at/wp_gal/wp_gal.vii.html
- Bible Hub connects the verse with Isaiah 40:31 and says perseverance is part of faith. https://biblehub.com/galatians/6.htm

**v. 10**
- Robertson: "let us do good" means keep on doing it. Believers come first because they belong to the same family. https://ccel.org/ccel/robertson_at/wp_gal/wp_gal.vii.html
- MacLaren notes that the word for "opportunity" here is the same as "time" in verse 9. https://biblehub.com/study/galatians/6-11.htm

**v. 11 (several readings)**
- Older commentators (Barnes, Gill, Clarke, Benson) took it as "how long a letter," meaning Paul wrote the whole letter himself as a sign of love. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/galatians/6-11.html Robertson says the Greek can't mean that. https://ccel.org/ccel/robertson_at/wp_gal/wp_gal.vii.html
- Weak eyesight (see 4:15): Jamieson-Fausset-Brown say this goes back to Jerome. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/galatians/6-11.htm Spurgeon and Scofield also supported it. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/galatians/6-11.html
- For emphasis: Robertson (following Ramsay) thinks this is most likely. https://ccel.org/ccel/robertson_at/wp_gal/wp_gal.vii.html Guzik agrees. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/galatians-6/
- D.A. Carson says failing eyesight is possible but not certain. The point is that readers hear Paul's own voice. https://thegospelcoalition.org/blogs/d-a-carson/1-kings-2-galatians-6-ezekiel-33-psalms-81-82

**v. 12**
- Robertson: the word for "make a good impression" means to look good in public (literally "fair of face"). "Compel" means they are *trying* to compel. https://ccel.org/ccel/robertson_at/wp_gal/wp_gal.vii.html
- Bible Hub: the Judaizers wanted to avoid persecution from strict Jewish circles. https://biblehub.com/galatians/6.htm

**v. 13**
- Robertson thinks the original wording probably means "those who are having themselves circumcised." https://ccel.org/ccel/robertson_at/wp_gal/wp_gal.vii.html
- Bible Hub sums up their motive as "boasting in your flesh," meaning bragging about converts. https://biblehub.com/galatians/6.htm

**v. 14**
- Robertson: Paul's wording expresses a strong wish that he never boast in anything else. "Has been crucified" means the world stays dead to him. He calls the verse one of Paul's great sayings, and says Paul's old world of Jewish descent is now dead to him. https://ccel.org/ccel/robertson_at/wp_gal/wp_gal.vii.html
- The BSB has a footnote: "through which" can also be read "through whom." https://biblehub.com/galatians/6.htm

**v. 15**
- Bible Hub and Robertson both link "new creation" to 2 Corinthians 5:17. https://biblehub.com/galatians/6.htm and https://ccel.org/ccel/robertson_at/wp_gal/wp_gal.vii.html

**v. 16 (the biggest disagreement)**
- **The church, Jews and Gentiles together.** Calvin says the phrase covers all believers, Jew or Gentile, united in one church. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/galatians/6-16.html Gill takes it as a further description of the same people, the spiritual Israel. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/galatians/6-16.html Ellicott says "and" here means "namely," and the phrase covers everyone with a faith like Abraham's. https://biblehub.com/galatians/6-16.htm Wesley, as quoted by Coffman, says it is the church of every nation that walks by this rule. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/galatians/6-16.html
- **Sam Storms (charismatic Reformed)** holds the same view and quotes Schreiner. He argues the church doesn't *replace* Israel but carries on the believing remnant. https://www.samstorms.org/enjoying-god-blog/post/-the-israel-of-god-in-galatians-6:16-and-the-question-of-replacement-theology
- **Jewish believers only (dispensational).** MacArthur, Ryrie, Henry Morris and William MacDonald take it to mean Jewish Christians, a separate group from the Gentile believers. https://www.preceptaustin.org/the_israel_of_god Constable adds that the repeated "upon" signals a second group, and that "Israel" means physical Jews everywhere else in the New Testament. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/galatians/6-16.html
- **Vincent's word study** sets out both options: "and" can join two groups or explain one. https://www.preceptaustin.org/the_israel_of_god
- **Burton's view**, as cited by Horner, is the pious Jewish remnant, including some who hadn't yet seen the truth as Paul did. https://www.preceptaustin.org/the_israel_of_god

**v. 17 (a Protestant/Catholic difference)**
- **Protestant reading:** the scars of his beatings, which work like a brand marking a slave. Gill says Paul means real scars, not the wounds in Christ's hands, feet and side. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/cjb/galatians/6-17.html Robertson links the marks to scourgings, and notes slaves, soldiers and pagan devotees were all branded. https://ccel.org/ccel/robertson_at/wp_gal/wp_gal.vii.html
- Guzik rejects the "mystical stigmata" reading as reading too much into the text and encouraging unhealthy mysticism. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/galatians-6/ GotQuestions agrees Paul didn't literally bear crucifixion wounds. https://www.gotquestions.org/stigmata.html
- **Catholic background:** the Catholic Public Domain Version translates it "the stigmata of the Lord Jesus." https://biblehub.com/galatians/6-17.htm Ellicott finds no direct link to St Francis of Assisi's stigmata. He thinks the Latin Bible's untranslated word "stigmata" probably shaped the idea. https://biblehub.com/galatians/6-17.htm

**v. 18**
- Robertson: this farewell is the same as in Philemon 25. Paul still calls them "brothers" after all his sharp words. https://ccel.org/ccel/robertson_at/wp_gal/wp_gal.vii.html
- Bible Hub: the letter opens with grace (1:3) and closes with it. https://biblehub.com/galatians/6.htm
